claims.text: In adjusted analyses, spending more than 3 hours per day on social media compared with no use is significantly associated with internalizing problems alone among adolescents.
In adjusted analyses, spending more than 3 hours per day on social media compared with no use is significantly associated with comorbid internalizing and externalizing problems among adolescents.
In adjusted analyses, social media use is not significantly associated with externalizing problems alone among adolescents.

evidence.description: Adjusted RRR for >3 to ≤6 hours was 1.60 (95% CI, 1.11-2.31) and for >6 hours was 1.78 (95% CI, 1.15-2.77) for internalizing problems alone.
Adjusted RRR for >3 to ≤6 hours was 2.01 (95% CI, 1.51-2.66) and for >6 hours was 2.44 (95% CI, 1.73-3.43) for comorbid internalizing and externalizing problems.
Adjusted analyses showed no significant association between social media use and externalizing problems alone.

methodologies.name: Longitudinal cohort analysis of PATH study data
methodologies.description: A longitudinal study of 6,595 US adolescents using waves 1-3 of the PATH study to examine daily social media use and subsequent mental health problems.
datasets: Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study
conditions: US adolescents aged 12-15 years at wave 1
Social media exposure measured at wave 2
Internalizing and externalizing problems measured at wave 3 using Global Appraisal of Individual Needs-Short Screener

limitations.text: Few longitudinal studies have investigated the prospective association between social media use and adolescent mental health problems.
No prior studies have quantified the proportion of mental health problems among adolescents attributable to social media use.

future_work.text: Determine whether setting limits on daily social media use is an effective means of reducing mental health problems in adolescents.
Determine whether increasing media literacy effectively reduces the burden of mental health problems in adolescents.
Determine whether redesigning social media platforms effectively reduces adolescent mental health problems.
